strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether SAM’s generalization gains carry membership-privacy costs. Examining performance across influence-based groups provides an interesting exploratory perspective beyond aggregate accuracy.

Experiments cover four image and tabular benchmarks, several attack methods, and additional ResNet18 and InceptionV4 architectures. The reported increases in single-query attack accuracy warrant further investigation.

SharpReg is simple to implement and reports substantial attack-accuracy reductions. Hyperparameter studies, comparisons with existing defenses, and appendix implementation details help assess the proposed tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is not established. Section 3 uses precomputed SGD influence scores on CIFAR-100 without directly measuring SAM’s memorization or connecting per-example memorization changes to attack success. Better performance on these harder, SGD-defined groups could reflect improved representations or greater accuracy headroom rather than increased memorization. Actual sharpness is also not measured to establish the proposed causal chain.

The entropy metric needs a sounder definition and validation. Equation (3) has a zero denominator when all influence scores vanish, yet Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 such examples to the highest-entropy bucket. Sensitivity to this convention, influence-estimation noise, and the manually selected bucket boundaries is untested. These choices affect a substantial portion of the central analysis.

Attack reporting needs reconciliation. For balanced member/nonmember evaluation, Equation (8) implies correctness-attack accuracy of approximately (training accuracy + 1 − test accuracy)/2. The CIFAR-100 SGD accuracies in Table 4 imply 59.84%, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. Actual attack-subset sizes, class balance, and any differences between the implemented attacks and their definitions must be clarified.

The privacy conclusion is broader than the evidence. Table 1 shows lower label-only attack accuracy for SAM on CIFAR-100 (69.18% to 65.41%) and CIFAR-10 (56.36% to 54.01%). The Purchase-100 single-query increase is only 0.29 percentage points, small relative to the reported variability. Calibrated attacks such as LiRA, low-false-positive-rate results, and clearly documented repetitions across independently trained victim models would strengthen the assessment.

SharpReg’s additional regularizer lacks an independent justification. For xi < 1, Equation (5) is exactly Equation (4) with lambda replaced by lambda/(1 − xi), multiplied by (1 − xi). Although Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter redundancy, the experiments do not control for effective sharpness weight and optimization scale. Consequently, they do not establish the claimed separate mechanism for encouraging nonzero training loss.

The defense contribution does not demonstrate a compelling accuracy–privacy frontier. In Table 4, the selected CIFAR-100 SharpReg configuration is dominated by SELENA in test accuracy and both attack metrics; the same holds on Texas-100. Comparisons against matched-utility, regularized or early-stopped SGD frontiers are missing, and the proposed computational advantage is not quantified.
